text: Alpha diversity measures diversity within single sample. ecodive, metrics grouped categories based aspect diversity quantify.

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Richness metrics estimate number distinct features (e.g., genera) sample. simplest metric, observed(), counts features non-zero abundance. Chao1 estimator extends inferring number unobserved, low-abundance features based ratio singletons (counts == 1) doubletons (counts == 2). default, chao1() bias-corrected estimator, scikit-bio QIIME 2. chao1(bias_corrected = FALSE) gives classic formula, larger doubletons.
code: # Equivalent to rowSums(counts > 0) observed(counts) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool  #>      4      3      4      5 # Infers 3 unobserved genera chao1(c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 5, 5, 5)) #> [1] 11  # Infers no unobserved genera chao1(c(1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5)) #> [1] 8  chao1(counts) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool  #>      4      3      4     11

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Diversity metrics account richness evenness (equally abundances distributed). Simpson’s index often used measure evenness, representing probability two randomly selected individuals belong different species. Shannon diversity index (entropy) another common metric weights richness evenness.
code: # High Evenness (0.8) vs Low Evenness (0.07) simpson(c(20, 20, 20, 20, 20)) #> [1] 0.8 simpson(c(100, 1, 1, 1, 1)) #> [1] 0.07507396  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(simpson(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.02302037 0.18806133 0.50725478 0.63539593 # High richness, High evenness shannon(rep(100, 100)) #> [1] 4.60517  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(shannon(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.07927797 0.35692121 0.74119910 1.10615349

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Dominance metrics focus abundance common species. Berger-Parker index proportional abundance single abundant feature.
code: # Stool is dominated by Bacteroides (341/345 counts -> ~0.99) # Nose is more balanced; Corynebacterium is max (171/345 counts -> ~0.49) sort(berger(counts)) #>      Nose    Saliva      Gums     Stool  #> 0.4956522 0.5217391 0.8956522 0.9884058

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Evenness metrics measure equally observed features share sample, apart many . Pielou’s evenness Shannon’s entropy divided largest possible value, \ln n n observed features; QIIME 2’s core-metrics reports . heip(), simpson_evenness() mcintosh_evenness() evenness indices.
code: # Perfectly even (1) vs dominated by one genus (0.13) pielou(c(20, 20, 20, 20, 20)) #> [1] 1 pielou(c(100, 1, 1, 1, 1)) #> [1] 0.1344212  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(pielou(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.04925817 0.32488369 0.53466213 0.79792108

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Hill numbers ^qD “effective number species”: many equally abundant features give diversity. order q sets much weight abundant features get, unifies common indices: q = 0 richness, q = 1 exponential Shannon’s entropy, q = 2 inverse Simpson index, q = \infty inverse Berger-Parker index. renyi() tsallis() entropies orders.

title: Alpha Diversity
text: rarefaction curve shows sample’s diversity subsampled ever smaller depths. curve levels says sample sequenced deeply enough; curves also help choose depth rarefy . rarefaction_curve() computes richness exactly (expected number features random subsample, standard deviation), metric rarefying times times depth. Every row also expected sample coverage depth. Use unrarefied counts:
code: rarefaction_curve(ex_counts, n_depths = 5) #> # A data.frame: 17 × 6 #> # Rarefaction curves #>    sample metric   depth value    sd coverage #>    <chr>  <chr>    <int> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> #>  1 Saliva observed     1  1    0        0.491 #>  2 Saliva observed   253  3.66 0.51     0.996 #>  3 Saliva observed   345  4    0        0.997 #>  4 Gums   observed     1  1    0        0.811 #>  5 Gums   observed   253  3.31 0.774    0.996 #>  6 Gums   observed   506  4.11 0.722    0.997 #>  7 Gums   observed   758  4.71 0.497    0.998 #>  8 Gums   observed   886  5    0        0.998 #>  9 Nose   observed     1  1    0        0.359 #> 10 Nose   observed   253  4.87 0.702    0.997 #> 11 Nose   observed   506  5.5  0.611    0.998 #> 12 Nose   observed   758  5.88 0.342    0.999 #> 13 Nose   observed  1011  6    0        1 #> 14 Stool  observed     1  1    0        0.987 #> 15 Stool  observed   253  2.65 0.982    0.993 #> 16 Stool  observed   506  4.29 0.762    0.993 #> 17 Stool  observed   615  5    0        0.994 #> # Attributes: totals, analytic, times, average  # Shannon diversity by resampling; a line at a planned depth of 345. rc <- rarefaction_curve(ex_counts, c('observed', 'shannon')) plot(rc, 'shannon', depth = 345)  # Rarefy each sample to 99.5% expected coverage instead of one depth. # Stool's estimated coverage (99.4%) falls short, so it is dropped. rowSums(rarefy(ex_counts, coverage = 0.995)) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  #>    220    136    120

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Given: n : Number features (e.g. species, OTUs, ASVs). X_i : Integer count -th feature. X_T : Total counts (sequencing depth). X_T = \sum_{=1}^{n} X_i P_i : Proportional abundance -th feature. P_i = X_i / X_T F_1 : Number singletons (X_i = 1). F_2 : Number doubletons (X_i = 2). H : Shannon’s entropy, -\sum_{=1}^{n} P_i \ln P_i. q : order Hill number entropy (q, default 2).

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Given: r : Rare cutoff (features \le r counts considered rare). F_{rare} : Number rare features. F_{abund} : Number abundant features (> r counts). X_{rare} : Total counts belonging rare features. C_{ace} : Sample abundance coverage estimator. \gamma_{ace}^2 : Estimated coefficient variation. C_{ace} = 1 - \frac{F_1}{X_{rare}} \gamma_{ace}^2 = \max\left[\frac{F_{rare} \sum_{=1}^{r}(-1)F_i}{C_{ace}X_{rare}(X_{rare} - 1)} - 1, 0\right] D_{ace} = F_{abund} + \frac{F_{rare}}{C_{ace}} + \frac{F_1}{C_{ace}}\gamma_{ace}^2

code: I am analyzing the [PACKAGE_NAME] R package to compare the number of ecologically relevant alpha and beta diversity metrics it provides. The package's reference manual is attached.   Please act as an expert in ecological bioinformatics. Carefully read the manual and adhere to these rules:  1. DEFINITION OF A SUITABLE METRIC:    - ECOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Only include metrics used to quantify community diversity. This includes measures of richness, evenness, dominance, turnover, or nestedness.    - SYMMETRY REQUIREMENT: Strictly ignore any asymmetric metrics (where $d(a, b) \neq d(b, a)$). All included beta diversity metrics must be symmetric.    - EXCLUSIONS: Do NOT count accessory functions, data manipulation, plotting functions, or general statistical correlations (e.g., Pearson/Spearman) unless they are explicitly implemented as a community diversity or dissimilarity index.  2. DISTINCTNESS RULE:    - ARGUMENTS AS METRICS: If a single function computes different named metrics based on a character argument (e.g., `method="bray"` vs `method="jaccard"`), each valid method counts as a SEPARATE metric.    - NAMED METRIC SELECTORS: If a numeric parameter (like q, alpha, or p) is used to dial in specific named indices (e.g., q=0 for Richness, q=1 for Shannon, q=2 for Simpson, or phylogenetic equivalents like Faith's PD, Allen's H, and Rao's Q), count each named case as a distinct metric. Do not count intermediate or arbitrary numeric values.    - THE BINARY TOGGLE: Treat the presence-absence version and abundance-based version of the same metric as ONE entity, unless they are provided as separate functions or separate named methods in a list.    - UNIFRAC EXCEPTION: Count unweighted, weighted, weighted normalized, generalized, and variance-adjusted UniFrac as separate metrics if explicitly supported.  3. CATEGORIZATION:    - ALPHA DIVERSITY: Metrics that quantify the diversity of a single sample or site (inventory diversity).    - BETA DIVERSITY: Metrics that quantify the difference or dissimilarity between a pair of samples (differentiation diversity).  To ensure accuracy, format your response as follows:  - **Candidate Extraction:** List all potential diversity functions and their associated methods/parameters found in the manual. - **Evaluation:** Filter the candidates against the "Symmetry," "Ecological Relevance," and "Distinctness" rules. - **Categorized Metric List:** Provide a table or list of all validated metrics with two columns: [Metric Name] and [Category (Alpha or Beta)]. - **Final Summary:**     - **Total Alpha Diversity Metrics:** [Integer]     - **Total Beta Diversity Metrics:** [Integer]     - **UniFrac Metrics Present:** [Yes/No]

text: Simulated data let us compare every method truth. Forty stool samples, 20 controls 20 treated, contain 150 taxa (ASVs). treated group five abundant taxa bloom 8-fold taxa 6–10 drop 4-fold, absolute terms; 140 taxa don’t change. sample “sequenced”: composition sampled random depth 5,000–40,000 reads, sequencer .
code: library(ecodive)  set.seed(42) n_taxa <- 150 groups <- rep(c('control', 'treated'), each = 20) n      <- length(groups) taxa   <- sprintf('ASV%03d', seq_len(n_taxa)) samples <- sprintf('S%02d', seq_len(n))  # Typical absolute abundance of each taxon: heavy-tailed, sorted so that # ASV001 is the most abundant. base <- sort(exp(rnorm(n_taxa, mean = 0, sd = 2)), decreasing = TRUE)  # True fold changes in absolute abundance (treated vs control). fold <- rep(1, n_taxa) fold[1:5]  <- 8      # blooms fold[6:10] <- 1 / 4  # declines changed    <- fold != 1  # Absolute abundances: the group effect, plus biological noise, plus # patchy absences of the rarer taxa. absolute <- t(sapply(groups, function (g) {   mu <- if (g == 'treated') base * fold else base   mu * exp(rnorm(n_taxa, 0, 0.5)) })) patchy <- matrix(runif(n * n_taxa) < 0.3, n, n_taxa) patchy[, 1:20] <- FALSE absolute[patchy] <- 0 dimnames(absolute) <- list(samples, taxa)  # Total microbial load (e.g. cells per gram), which in a real study would # have to be measured separately. load <- rowSums(absolute)  # Sequencing: draw reads from each sample's composition. depth  <- round(runif(n, 5000, 40000)) counts <- t(sapply(seq_len(n), function (i) rmultinom(1, depth[i], absolute[i, ]))) dimnames(counts) <- list(samples, taxa)  counts[1:5, 1:6] #>     ASV001 ASV002 ASV003 ASV004 ASV005 ASV006 #> S01   8584   1695   4009   1480   1236    461 #> S02   7078   4514   1776   1924   1166    705 #> S03   3198   2471   1677   1102   1150    571 #> S04   6436   3919   3026   2170    959   1674 #> S05   4966   1842   2315   2375    618   1273 mean(counts == 0)  # proportion of zeros #> [1] 0.3563333  # Taxa found in at least 90% of samples, for the steps that need them. prevalent <- colMeans(counts > 0) >= 0.9 sum(prevalent) #> [1] 20

title: Compositional Analysis of Microbiome Data
text: Compositional methods recover ratios, never totals. measure sample’s total microbial load (flow cytometry, total 16S qPCR, spike-), can estimate absolute abundances instead: quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP; Vandeputte et al. 2017). simplest version multiplies relative abundances load (Jian et al. 2020); Vandeputte’s original first rarefies every sample number reads per cell. Loads predicted relative profile (Nishijima et al. 2025) can passed qmp_scale() , prediction measurement: computed relative profile, (infer) can’t confirm compositional result (see qmp_scale()’s help, “Predicted loads”). load measured 20% error, real measurement : Relative abundances make unchanged taxa look depleted; load, close zero . qmp_rarefy() pays even detection limit reads: every sample cut number reads per cell, keeps 720 7,386 reads per sample. QMP data absolute abundances, compositions, analyse ordinary methods (e.g. bray(q_rarefy)), clr, remove load . Used practice. Vandeputte et al. (2017) combined 16S sequencing flow-cytometric cell counts found tenfold differences microbial load healthy people; Vandeputte et al. (2021) followed 20 women daily six weeks QMP. Props et al. (2017) showed flow cytometry rising relative abundance needn’t mean growth. Spike-ins way measure load: Stämmler et al. (2016) added three bacteria stool samples stem-cell transplant patients, Tkacz et al. (2018) added synthetic DNA soils.

title: Compositional Analysis of Microbiome Data
text: Two extensions RPCA gemelli package planned: Compositional tensor factorization (ctf(); Martino et al. 2021) arranges samples subjects × taxa × time points separates differences subjects changes time. Joint-RPCA (rpca_joint()) ordinates several tables measured samples (e.g. 16S, metagenomics metabolomics) shared sample scores. Used practice. CTF: Haskey et al. (2023), randomised diet trial ulcerative colitis repeated stool samples; Liao et al. (2023), vaginal metagenomes across pregnancy preterm birth. Joint-RPCA (Cordazzo Vargas et al. 2026): Burcham et al. (2024) integrated 16S, 18S, metagenome-assembled genomes metabolomics decomposition soils; Tang-Wing et al. (2024) linked metagenomic metabolomic features marmosets diet change.

title: Introduction to ecodive
text: ex_counts feature table 345 saliva observations, nose 1011 observations. unequal sampling depth can cause systematic biases. title: Performance Guide
text: Many diversity metrics operate transformed data, commonly relative abundances (norm = 'percent'). specify transformation like norm = 'percent', ecodive performs conversion internally. adds small amount computational overhead. plan run many different analyses transformed data, efficient perform transformation pass pre-transformed data ecodive, specifying norm = 'none'.

title: Performance Guide
text: one exception rule centered log-ratio transformation (norm = 'clr'), used calculating Aitchison distance. standard CLR workflow requires replacing zeros small pseudocount transformation (since log(0) undefined). replacement step instantly turns sparse matrix (mostly zeros) fully dense matrix (zeros), dramatically increases memory consumption. ecodive’s implementation CLR-compatible beta diversity metrics pseudocount-aware. Instead modifying entire matrix memory, C engine applies pseudocount dynamically distance calculation. allows input matrix remain sparse enables algorithm work directly original data pointer without creating massive, dense copy matrix object. Therefore, CLR-based metrics, achieve significantly better performance lower memory usage letting ecodive handle transformation. : :
code: # Best for CLR: Let ecodive handle the transformation dynamically aitchison_dist <- aitchison(optimal_counts, margin = 2L, pseudocount = 0.5) # Inefficient for CLR: Adding pseudocounts creates a dense matrix library(compositions) dense_matrix   <- clr(t(as.matrix(optimal_counts)) + 0.5) # Becomes dense aitchison_dist <- euclidean(dense_matrix, norm = 'none')

title: Statistical Tests
text: PERMANOVA can also give small p-value groups center different spreads. permdisp() tests spread ; significant result means PERMANOVA difference may come partly wholly dispersion.  three species equally spread, PERMANOVA result reflects real difference centers. warning comes Bray-Curtis distances Euclidean: flower can sit negative squared distance species’ center, permdisp() sets zero (Anderson 2006).
code: res <- permdisp(dm, 'Species', iris) #> Warning: Some squared distances to group centres are negative, and were set to #> 0. res #> Homogeneity of multivariate dispersions (PERMDISP) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> F = 0.5676, p = 0.573, z = -0.4401 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Distances to group centroids: #>     setosa versicolor  virginica  #>    0.03781    0.04248    0.04103  #>  #>            Df  Sum Sq   Mean Sq     F N.Perm Pr(>F) #> Groups      2 0.00057 0.0002852 0.568    999  0.573 #> Residuals 147 0.07386 0.0005024 plot(res)

title: Statistical Tests
text: anosim() compares ranks distances within groups. R near 1 means every group distinct, near 0 means difference. mrpp() compares average distance within groups random groups give. plot() MRPP result shows group’s mean within-group distance, weighted mean (observed \delta) mean distances (\delta expected chance); type = 'null' shows permutations instead, tests.
code: anosim(dm, 'Species', iris) #> Analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> R = 0.8576, p = 0.001, z =  79.4 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Mean rank of the distances, between and within groups: #>            pairs mean_rank #> Between     7500   7163.90 #> setosa      1225   2239.66 #> versicolor  1225   2457.85 #> virginica   1225   2418.15  res <- mrpp(dm, 'Species', iris) res #> Multi-response permutation procedure (MRPP) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> delta = 0.05795, p = 0.001, z = -78.9 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Mean within-group distances (weights: n): #>        setosa versicolor virginica #> delta 0.05502     0.0602   0.05861 #> n          50         50        50 #>  #> Expected delta: 0.158 #> Chance-corrected within-group agreement A: 0.6332 plot(res)

text: overall test finds groups differ, next question usually ones. pairwise = TRUE reruns test pair groups’ samples, adjusts pairs’ p-values multiple testing (Holm’s method default; p_adjust = 'BH' controls false discovery rate instead). overall result unchanged. p_value pair’s permutation p-value, p_adjusted value report. anosim() mrpp() take arguments, permdisp() adds adjusted p-values pairwise t tests:

title: Statistical Tests
text: mantel() correlates dm numeric variable, second distance matrix: , whether flowers similar petals also similar sepals. method can 'pearson', 'spearman', 'kendall'.  mantel_partial() removes effect third set distances, given: , whether sepals petals still match accounting petal width alone.

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2005: Unweighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: unweighted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: unweighted_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=FALSE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=FALSE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric unweighted_unifrac mothur: unifrac.unweighted() First, transform B presence (1) absence (0) indicators. \begin{align*}  &= \{9, 0, 0, 0, 9, 6, 3, 3\} \\ ' &= \{1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1\} \end{align*} \begin{align*} B  &= \{7, 5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 8, 0\} \\ B' &= \{1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0\} \end{align*} apply formula: \begin{align*} U &= \displaystyle \frac{\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(|'_i - B'_i|)}{\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(max('_i,B'_i))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{L_1(|'_1-B'_1|) + L_2(|'_2-B'_2|) + \cdots + L_n(|'_n-B'_n|)}{L_1(max('_1,B'_1)) + L_2(max('_2,B'_2)) + \cdots + L_n(max('_n,B'_n))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.2(|1-1|) + 0.4(|0-1|) + \cdots + 0.3(|1-0|)}{0.2(max(1,1)) + 0.4(max(0,1)) + \cdots + 0.3(max(1,0))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.2(0) + 0.4(1) + 0.8(1) + 0.5(1) + 0.9(0) + 0.6(0) + 0.7(0) + 0.3(1)}{0.2(1) + 0.4(1) + 0.8(1) + 0.5(1) + 0.9(1) + 0.6(1) + 0.7(1) + 0.3(1)}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.4 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.3}{0.2 + 0.4 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.6 + 0.7 + 0.3}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{2}{4.4}  \\ \\ U &= 0.4545455 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2007: Raw Weighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: weighted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: weighted_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=FALSE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=FALSE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_unifrac \begin{align*} W &= \sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|  \\ \\ W &= L_1|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}| + L_2|\frac{A_2}{A_T} - \frac{B_2}{B_T}| + \cdots + L_n|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|  \\ \\ W &= 0.2|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}| + 0.4|\frac{0}{15} - \frac{5}{15}| + \cdots + 0.3|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|  \\ \\ W &= 0.02\overline{6} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.42 + 0.08 + 0.2\overline{3} + 0.06  \\ \\ W &= 1.14 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2007: Normalized Weighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: normalized_unifrac() R Package abdiv: weighted_normalized_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=TRUE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=TRUE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_normalized_unifrac mothur: unifrac.weighted() \begin{align*}  N &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|}   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {L_1|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}| + L_2|\frac{A_2}{A_T} - \frac{B_2}{B_T}| + \cdots + L_n|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|}   {L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}) + L_2(\frac{A_2}{A_T} + \frac{B_2}{B_T}) + \cdots + L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {0.2|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}| + 0.4|\frac{0}{15} - \frac{5}{15}| + \cdots + 0.3|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|}   {0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}) + 0.4(\frac{0}{15} + \frac{5}{15}) + \cdots + 0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {0.02\overline{6} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.42 + 0.08 + 0.2\overline{3} + 0.06}   {0.21\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.66 + 0.56 + 0.51\overline{3} + 0.06}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac{1.14}{2.326667}  \\ \\ N &= 0.4899713 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Chen et al. 2012: Generalized UniFrac R Package ecodive: generalized_unifrac(alpha = 0.5) R Package abdiv: generalized_unifrac(alpha = 0.5) R Package GUniFrac: GUniFrac(alpha = 0.5) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric generalized_unifrac -0.5 \begin{align*}  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})^{\alpha}     |\displaystyle \frac       {\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}}       {\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T}} |}   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})^{\alpha}}  \\ \\  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {     L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}}         {\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}}| +     \cdots +     L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}}         {\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T}}|   }{     L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T})^{0.5} +     \cdots +     L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})^{0.5}   }     \\ \\  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {     0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}}         {\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}}| +     \cdots +     0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}}         {\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15}}|   }{     0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15})^{0.5} +     \cdots +     0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})^{0.5}   }     \\ \\    G &\approx \displaystyle \frac   {0.03 + 0.23 + 0.21 + 0.26 + 0.49 + 0.08 + 0.27 + 0.13}   {0.21 + 0.23 + 0.21 + 0.26 + 0.77 + 0.58 + 0.60 + 0.13}   \\ \\    G &= \displaystyle \frac{1.701419}{2.986235}  \\ \\ G &= 0.569754  \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Chang et al, 2011: Variance Adjusted Weighted (VAW) UniFrac R Package ecodive: variance_adjusted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: variance_adjusted_unifrac() qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_normalized_unifrac --p-variance-adjusted \begin{align*}  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_i + B_i)(A_T + B_T - A_i - B_i)}} }   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_i + B_i)(A_T + B_T - A_i - B_i)}} }  \\ \\  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {     L_1\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_1 + B_1)(A_T + B_T - A_1 - B_1)}} +     \cdots +     L_n\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_n + B_n)(A_T + B_T - A_n - B_n)}}   }{     L_1\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_1 + B_1)(A_T + B_T - A_1 - B_1)}} +     \cdots +     L_n\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_n + B_n)(A_T + B_T - A_n - B_n)}}   }     \\ \\  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {     0.2\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}|}     {\sqrt{(9 + 7)(15 + 15 - 9 - 7)}} +     \cdots +     0.3\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|}     {\sqrt{(3 + 0)(15 + 15 - 3 - 0)}}   }{     0.2\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}}     {\sqrt{(9 + 7)(15 + 15 - 9 - 7)}} +     \cdots +     0.3\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15}}     {\sqrt{(3 + 0)(15 + 15 - 3 - 0)}}   }     \\ \\    V &\approx \displaystyle \frac   {0.002 + 0.012 + 0.010 + 0.013 + 0.029 + 0.005 + 0.016 + 0.007}   {0.014 + 0.012 + 0.010 + 0.013 + 0.046 + 0.037 + 0.036 + 0.007}   \\ \\    V &= \displaystyle \frac{4.09389}{4.174402}  \\ \\ V &= 0.9807128  \end{align*}

title: Parallel and Memory-Efficient Ecological Diversity Analysis
text: Analyzing ecological diversity often computational bottleneck, especially large datasets. ecodive addresses providing: High Performance: ecodive written C parallelized using pthreads, making dramatically faster R packages. Benchmarks show can 14,000x faster use 200,000x less memory. Zero Dependencies: package external R dependencies, making lightweight, stable, easy install. also makes ideal secure backend R packages. Comprehensive Metrics: implements 14 alpha 38 beta diversity metrics, including classic phylogenetic-aware methods like Faith’s PD, complete UniFrac family compositional PhILR distance. Ordination Statistics: Ten ordination methods (PCoA, NMDS, UMAP, t-SNE, db-RDA, robust Aitchison PCA, ), biplots, five permutation tests (PERMANOVA, PERMDISP, ANOSIM, MRPP, Mantel), whole analysis needs package. Trusted Results: Every method tested established package replaces, vegan, ape, scikit-bio, scikit-learn, uwot, gemelli. Results identical number threads, random methods take seed. Ease Use: API simple integrates seamlessly popular bioinformatics packages like phyloseq rbiom.

title: Abundance-based Coverage Estimator (ACE) — ace
text: ACE metric separates features "abundant" "rare" groups based cutoff (usually 10 counts). assumes presence abundant species certain, true number rare species must estimated. Equations: $$C_{ace} = 1 - \frac{F_1}{X_{rare}}$$ $$\gamma_{ace}^2 = \max\left[\frac{F_{rare} \sum_{=1}^{r}(-1)F_i}{C_{ace}X_{rare}(X_{rare} - 1)} - 1, 0\right]$$ $$D_{ace} = F_{abund} + \frac{F_{rare}}{C_{ace}} + \frac{F_1}{C_{ace}}\gamma_{ace}^2$$ : \(r\) : Rare cutoff (default 10). Features \(\le r\) counts considered rare. \(F_i\) : Number features exactly \(\) counts. \(F_1\) : Number features \(X_i = 1\) (singletons). \(F_{rare}\) : Number rare features \(X_i \le r\). \(F_{abund}\) : Number abundant features \(X_i > r\). \(X_{rare}\) : Total counts belonging rare features. \(C_{ace}\) : sample abundance coverage estimator. \(\gamma_{ace}^2\) : estimated coefficient variation. Parameter: cutoff integer threshold distinguishing rare abundant species. Standard practice use 10.

title: Aitchison distance — aitchison
text: Aitchison distance defined : $$\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^{n} [(\ln{X_i} - X_L) - (\ln{Y_i} - Y_L)]^2}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute counts \(\)-th feature. \(X_L\), \(Y_L\) : Mean log abundances. \(X_L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{=1}^{n} \ln{X_i}\). \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- log((x + pseudocount) / exp(mean(log(x + pseudocount)))) y <- log((y + pseudocount) / exp(mean(log(y + pseudocount)))) sqrt(sum((x-y)^2)) # Euclidean distance

title: Aitchison distance — aitchison
text: Zeros undefined Aitchison (CLR) transformation. pseudocount NULL (default) zeros detected, function uses half minimum non-zero value (min(x[x>0]) / 2) issues warning. suppress warning, provide explicit value (e.g., 1). matters: choice pseudocount neutral; acts weighting factor can significantly distort downstream results, especially sparse datasets. See Gloor et al. (2017) Kaul et al. (2017) open-access discussions mathematical implications, Costea et al. (2014) impact community clustering.

title: Alpha Diversity Wrapper Function — alpha_div
text: counts numeric matrix count data (samples \(\times\) features). Typically contains absolute abundances (integer counts), though proportions also accepted. metric name alpha diversity metric. One c('ace', 'berger', 'brillouin', 'chao1', 'dominance', 'faith', 'fisher', 'gini', 'goods_coverage', 'heip', 'hill', 'inv_simpson', 'margalef', 'mcintosh', 'mcintosh_evenness', 'menhinick', 'observed', 'pielou', 'renyi', 'shannon', 'simpson', 'simpson_evenness', 'squares', 'strong', 'tsallis'). Case-insensitive partial name matching supported, scikit-bio's names ('pielou_e', 'simpson_d', 'observed_features' 'enspie'). Programmatic access via list_metrics('alpha'). norm Normalize incoming counts. Options : 'none': transformation. 'percent': Relative abundance (sample abundances sum 1). 'hellinger': Square root relative abundance (Hellinger transformation). 'binary': Unweighted presence/absence (count either 0 1). 'clr': Centered log ratio. 'rclr': Robust centered log ratio. 'log': Log relative abundance (log-TSS), pseudocount added every value first. Default: 'none'. cutoff maximum number observations consider "rare". Default: 10. digits Precision returned values, number decimal places. E.g. default digits=3 return 6.392. tree phylo-class object representing phylogenetic tree OTUs counts. OTU identifiers given colnames(counts) must present tree. Can omitted tree embedded counts object attr(counts, 'tree'). margin margin containing samples. 1 samples rows, 2 samples columns. Ignored counts special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1 q order Hill number, Rényi's Tsallis's entropy: single number least 0, Inf allowed. used hill(), renyi() tsallis(). Default: 2, scikit-bio (calls order). bias_corrected Chao1 : use bias-corrected form (default, scikit-bio QIIME 2), classic form sample singletons doubletons (FALSE). See chao1(). cpus many parallel processing threads used. default, n_cpus(), CPU cores R process may use, within limits set . Results cpus.

title: Alpha Diversity Wrapper Function — alpha_div
text: metrics follow skbio.diversity.alpha (scikit-bio 0.7.4), QIIME 2's diversity alpha runs, differences: Logarithms natural. scikit-bio's shannon(), pielou_e() renyi() take base; divide ecodive's shannon() renyi() log(base) instead. Pielou's evenness depend base. finite option simpson(), dominance() inv_simpson() (scikit-bio's estimator without replacement). gini() index computed rectangles (scikit-bio's default method = "rectangles", "trapezoids"). sample observations NA every metric. scikit-bio gives nan metrics, 0 chao1() gini_index(). chao1(bias_corrected = FALSE) classic formula, falling back bias-corrected one sample singletons doubletons, exactly scikit-bio .

title: Chao1 Richness Estimator — chao1
text: Chao1 estimator uses ratio singletons doubletons estimate number missing species. default bias-corrected form (Chao 1987), scikit-bio QIIME 2: $$n + \frac{F_1 (F_1 - 1)}{2 (F_2 + 1)}$$ bias_corrected = FALSE, classic form (Chao 1984): $$n + \frac{(F_1)^2}{2 F_2}$$ infinite doubletons. , scikit-bio's chao1(bias_corrected = False), classic form used \(F_1 > 0\) \(F_2 > 0\), bias-corrected form otherwise. : \(n\) : number observed features. \(F_1\) : Number features observed (singletons). \(F_2\) : Number features observed twice (doubletons). vegan::estimateR() iNEXT multiply bias-corrected term \((N - 1)/N\), \(N\) number observations, estimates slightly smaller shallow samples singletons. ecodive version 2.4.0 used classic form without fallback, gave Inf without doubletons NaN without singletons doubletons. NA group methods. run: run's number, 0 base run. parameter: run changed: 'base', 'pseudocount', 'zeros', 'scale_sd', , crossed = TRUE, 'crossed' runs change one. setting: run's setting words, e.g. "pseudocount = 0.5", "zeros = mult", "pseudocount = 0.5, scale_sd = 1", "base". effect: method's effect size, column result named effect list_da_tests() (log_fc, log2_fc, median_diff, diff, estimate); NA ancom(), none. p_adjusted: method's adjusted p-value (NA ancom()). reject: method's decision, reject column (ANCOM-BC, reject_robust). Attributes: method: method's id, e.g. 'ancombc2'. effect_name: name method's effect column (NA ANCOM). alpha: base run's significance level. log_base: base effects' logs (exp(1), 2, NA effects logs). covariate: model methods, covariate term interest (first column groups's term, else first covariate intercept), plot() shows default; NULL group methods. runs: data frame runs, columns run, parameter, pseudocount, zeros, scale_sd (NA run keeps base run's) setting. fits: method's result every run, list run order (base run first). can take much memory: one full result per run. summary: data frame row per feature (covariate): feature, covariate, n_runs (runs result ), n_reject (reject ), prop_reject (proportion), passed (TRUE every run makes decision, rejected ), robust (passed rejected base run: decisions report), sign_stable (TRUE effect sign every run finite; NA without effects).

code: # Ten samples and two extraction blanks, with DNA concentrations.     # F1 and F2 are contaminants: a fixed amount of DNA, so their share     # falls as the concentration rises, and they fill the blanks.     set.seed(1)     conc   <- c(exp(seq(1, 4, length.out = 10)), 0.5, 0.6)     neg    <- rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), c(10, 2))     counts <- matrix(rpois(12 * 8, 200), 12, 8, dimnames = list(       c(paste0('S', 1:10), 'Blank1', 'Blank2'), paste0('F', 1:8) ))     counts[, 1:2] <- round(counts[, 1:2] * 5 / conc)     counts[11:12, 3:8] <- 0      # The frequency test     res <- decontam(counts, conc)     res #> # A data.frame: 8 × 9 #> # decontam (frequency) #>   feature  freq  prev prev_neg prev_pos   p_freq p_prev        p contaminant #>   <chr>   <dbl> <int>    <int>    <int>    <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>       <lgl> #> 1 F1      0.147    12       NA       NA 0.000587     NA 0.000587        TRUE #> 2 F2      0.151    12       NA       NA 0.000397     NA 0.000397        TRUE #> 3 F3      0.116    10       NA       NA 1            NA 1              FALSE #> 4 F4      0.116    10       NA       NA 1            NA 1              FALSE #> 5 F5      0.118    10       NA       NA 1            NA 1              FALSE #> 6 F6      0.117    10       NA       NA 1            NA 1              FALSE #> 7 F7      0.118    10       NA       NA 1            NA 1              FALSE #> 8 F8      0.117    10       NA       NA 1            NA 1              FALSE #> # Attributes: method, test, threshold, batch_combine, n_neg, n_pos      # Frequency and prevalence, combined     res <- decontam(counts, conc, neg)     res$feature[res$contaminant] #> [1] "F1" "F2"      # Remove them     clean <- counts[!neg, !res$contaminant]      # The values as columns of sample metadata     meta <- data.frame(dna = conc, blank = neg, row.names = rownames(counts))     res  <- decontam(counts, 'dna', 'blank', meta, method = 'prevalence')      # Low-biomass samples: the features that are not contaminants     decontam_not(counts, neg) #> # A data.frame: 8 × 8 #> # decontam_not (prevalence) #>   feature  freq  prev prev_neg prev_pos  p_prev       p not_contaminant #>   <chr>   <dbl> <int>    <int>    <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>           <lgl> #> 1 F1      0.147    12        2       10 0.5     0.5               FALSE #> 2 F2      0.151    12        2       10 0.5     0.5               FALSE #> 3 F3      0.116    10        0       10 0.00758 0.00758            TRUE #> 4 F4      0.116    10        0       10 0.00758 0.00758            TRUE #> 5 F5      0.118    10        0       10 0.00758 0.00758            TRUE #> 6 F6      0.117    10        0       10 0.00758 0.00758            TRUE #> 7 F7      0.118    10        0       10 0.00758 0.00758            TRUE #> 8 F8      0.117    10        0       10 0.00758 0.00758            TRUE #> # Attributes: method, test, threshold, n_neg, n_pos      # Plots     plot(res)      plot(res, 'prevalence')      decontam_frequency_plot(counts, c('F1', 'F5'), conc, neg)

code: # 40 samples: four environmental variables, two of which matter.     set.seed(1)     meta <- data.frame(       ph    = runif(40, 5, 8),       temp  = runif(40, 10, 20),       depth = runif(40),       site  = factor(rep(c('a', 'b', 'c', 'd'), 10)) )     counts <- matrix(rpois(40 * 15, 4), 40, 15)     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(10 * (meta$ph - 5))     counts[, 6:9] <- counts[, 6:9] + round(2 * (meta$temp - 10))      # tb-RDA on the Hellinger-normalized table.     fs <- forward_select(counts, ~ ph + temp + depth + site, meta, norm = 'hellinger')     fs #> Forward selection by RDA (hellinger): 40 samples #> Permutations: 999 (free) #> Global model: 6 df, adj. R-squared 0.6140, F = 11.34, p = 0.001 #>  #>   variable df r_squared r_squared_cum adj_r_squared adj_r_squared_cum     F #> 1       ph  1    0.4397        0.4397        0.4249            0.4249 29.82 #> 2     temp  1    0.1914        0.6311        0.1862            0.6112 19.20 #>   p_value #> 1   0.001 #> 2   0.001 #>  #> Stopped: adjusted R-squared would exceed the global model's. #> Next best: depth (adj. R-squared 0.6217) #> Selected: ~ph + temp     plot(fs)       # db-RDA on Bray-Curtis distances, then partition the variation.     fs <- forward_select(bray(counts), ~ ph + temp + depth + site, meta)     attr(fs, 'selected') #> ~ph + temp #> <environment: 0x60c7601777a0>     varpart(bray(counts), env = attr(fs, 'selected'), site = ~ site, data = meta) #> Variation partitioning by db-RDA: 40 samples, 2 sets #> Total inertia: 1.5469 #>  #>   env   attr(fs, "selected")    2 df, adj. R-squared 0.7798 #>   site  ~site                   3 df, adj. R-squared -0.0039 #>   All                           5 df, adj. title: Generalized UniFrac (GUniFrac) — generalized_unifrac
text: Generalized UniFrac distance defined : $$\frac{\sum_{=1}^{n} L_i(P_i + Q_i)^{\alpha}\left|\frac{P_i - Q_i}{P_i + Q_i}\right|}{\sum_{=1}^{n} L_i(P_i + Q_i)^{\alpha}}$$ : \(n\) : number branches tree. \(L_i\) : length \(\)-th branch. \(P_i\), \(Q_i\) : proportion community descending branch \(\) sample P Q. \(\alpha\) : scalable weighting factor. Parameter: alpha alpha parameter controls weight given abundant lineages. \(\alpha = 1\) corresponds Weighted UniFrac, \(\alpha = 0\) corresponds Unweighted UniFrac.

title: Gini Index — gini
text: Gini index computed Lorenz curve \(K\) features table, rectangles, scikit-bio's gini_index(): $$\max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{2}{K} \sum_{j = 1}^{K} L_j\right)$$ : \(K\) : number features table, including absent sample. \(L_j\) : Lorenz curve: share sample's total held \(j\) least abundant features, \(\sum_{\le j} X_{()} / X_T\), \(X_{(1)} \le \ldots \le X_{(K)}\) sorted abundances. Gini index depends many features table , including features sample lacks: absent feature makes sample look less even. Filtering features table (adding -zero ones) changes , compare samples table. sample one table \(K\) features, equally abundant, index 0; sample counts one feature index \(1 - 2/K\) (rectangles, Lorenz curve's area overestimated \(1/(2K)\)). alpha_div(counts, 'gini') index; Gini-Simpson index 'simpson'. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,] L <- cumsum(sort(x)) / sum(x) max(0, 1 - 2 * sum(L) / length(x))

title: Hill Numbers — hill
text: Hill number order \(q\) defined : $${}^qD = \left(\sum_{= 1}^{n} P_i^q\right)^{1/(1-q)}$$ limits \({}^1D = e^H\) (\(H\): Shannon's entropy) \({}^\infty D = 1 / \max(P_i)\). : \(n\) : number features. \(P_i\) : Proportional abundance \(\)-th feature. order sets much weight abundant features get. Hill numbers profile unifies common indices: \(q = 0\): richness, observed(). \(q = 1\): exponential Shannon's entropy, exp(shannon()), weighs every feature frequency (Jost 2006). \(q = 2\): inverse Simpson index, inv_simpson(). \(q = \infty\): inverse Berger-Parker index, 1 / berger(). default order, 2, scikit-bio's, makes hill() equal inv_simpson(); give q order. renyi() log(hill()), tsallis() another function . Observed Hill numbers grow sequencing depth, small \(q\); compare samples equal depth, instance alpha_div_rarefied(). Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,] q <- 2 p <- x[x > 0] / sum(x) sum(p ** q) ** (1 / (1 - q))

title: Mantel Test — mantel
code: # 30 samples along a pH gradient, which shifts the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     ph <- setNames(round(runif(30, 6, 8), 1), rownames(counts))     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (ph - 6))      dm <- bray(counts)      # Are samples that differ more in pH also more different in     # community composition?     res <- mantel(dm, ph)     res #> Mantel test (Pearson) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.593, p = 0.001, z = 9.786 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30     plot(res)       # With rank correlation.     mantel(dm, ph, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z =    10 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # The same as a column of sample metadata.     meta <- data.frame(row.names = rownames(counts), ph = ph)     mantel(dm, 'ph', data = meta, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z =    10 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # Two distance matrices.     mantel(dm, dist(counts[, 6:20])) #> Mantel test (Pearson) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.4893, p = 0.001, z = 6.502 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

title: Partial Mantel Test — mantel_partial
code: # 30 samples along a pH gradient, which shifts the first five genera,     # at random locations.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       ph  = round(runif(30, 6, 8), 1),       lat = runif(30, 30, 35),       lon = runif(30, -100, -95) )     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (meta$ph - 6))      dm  <- bray(counts)     geo <- dist(meta[, c('lat', 'lon')])      # Are samples that differ more in pH also more different in     # community composition, beyond the effect of geographic distance?     mantel_partial(dm, 'ph', given = geo, data = meta) #> Partial Mantel test (Pearson) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5931, p = 0.001, z = 9.759 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # With rank correlation.     mantel_partial(dm, 'ph', given = geo, data = meta, method = 'spearman') #> Partial Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z = 9.969 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # The same, through dist_test().     dist_test(dm, 'mantel_partial', 'ph', meta, given = geo, method = 'spearman') #> Partial Mantel test (Spearman) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z = 9.969 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

title: Minkowski distance — minkowski
text: Minkowski distance defined : $$\sqrt[p]{\sum_{=1}^{n} (X_i - Y_i)^p}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute abundances \(\)-th feature. \(n\) : number features. \(p\) : geometry space (power parameter). Parameter: power power parameter (default 1.5) determines value \(p\) equation. Special Cases Manhattan distance: \(p = 1\), formula reduces sum absolute differences. Euclidean distance: \(p = 2\), formula reduces standard straight-line distance. Chebyshev distance: \(p \\infty\), formula reduces maximum absolute difference. Base R Equivalent:
code: p <- 1.5 x <- ex_counts[1,] y <- ex_counts[2,] sum(abs(x - y)^p) ^ (1/p)

title: Morisita dissimilarity — morisita
text: Morisita dissimilarity defined : $$1 - \frac{2\sum_{=1}^{n}X_{}Y_{}}{\left(\frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}X_i(X_i - 1)}{X_T(X_T - 1)} + \frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}Y_i(Y_i - 1)}{Y_T(Y_T - 1)}\right)X_{T}Y_{T}}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute counts \(\)-th feature. \(X_T\), \(Y_T\) : Total counts sample. \(X_T = \sum_{=1}^{n} X_i\). \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,] y <- ex_counts[2,] simpson_x <- sum(x * (x - 1)) / (sum(x) * (sum(x) - 1)) simpson_y <- sum(y * (y - 1)) / (sum(y) * (sum(y) - 1)) 1 - ((2 * sum(x * y)) / ((simpson_x + simpson_y) * sum(x) * sum(y)))

The 'high' group has more     # of the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       treatment = rep(c('ctrl', 'low', 'high'), each = 10),       site      = rep(c('A', 'B'), 15) )     high <- meta$treatment == 'high'     counts[high, 1:5] <- counts[high, 1:5] + 5      dm <- bray(counts)      # Are samples more alike within treatment groups?     res <- mrpp(dm, 'treatment', meta)     res #> Multi-response permutation procedure (MRPP) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> delta = 0.2244, p = 0.001, z = -7.322 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Mean within-group distances (weights: n): #>         ctrl   high    low #> delta 0.2443 0.1757 0.2531 #> n         10     10     10 #>  #> Expected delta: 0.2438 #> Chance-corrected within-group agreement A: 0.07954      # Each group's mean within-group distance, and the permutations.     plot(res)      plot(res, type = 'null')       # The same, with the groups as a vector.     res <- mrpp(dm, meta$treatment)     as.data.frame(res) #>   test stat_name statistic p_value         z n_perm #> 1 mrpp     delta 0.2243903   0.001 -7.321666    999      # Permuting only within sites.     mrpp(dm, 'treatment', meta, strata = 'site') #> Multi-response permutation procedure (MRPP) of Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity #>  #> delta = 0.2244, p = 0.001, z = -7.342 #> Permutations: 999 (within strata) #>  #> Mean within-group distances (weights: n): #>         ctrl   high    low #> delta 0.2443 0.1757 0.2531 #> n         10     10     10 #>  #> Expected delta: 0.2438 #> Chance-corrected within-group agreement A: 0.07954      # Each pair of treatments, with Holm-adjusted p-values.     mrpp(dm, 'treatment', meta, pairwise = TRUE)$pairwise #>               delta           A         z  n n_perm p_value p_adjusted #> ctrl-high 0.2100255  0.11073465 -9.180235 20    999   0.001      0.003 #> ctrl-low  0.2487199 -0.01162824  1.182126 20    999   0.892      0.892 #> high-low  0.2144254  0.08957766 -7.820948 20    999   0.001      0.003

title: Normalize a Count Table — normalize
text: counts numeric matrix count data (samples \(\times\) features). Typically contains absolute abundances (integer counts), though proportions also accepted. norm transformation: 'percent': Relative abundance: sample's counts divided sum (sum 1). 'chord': sample's counts divided Euclidean norm (squares sum 1). 'hellinger': square root count divided sample's sum (Hellinger transformation). Euclidean distances results Hellinger distances. 'binary': Presence/absence: 1 non-zero count. 'clr': Centered log ratio: \(\log(x + pseudocount)\) minus sample's mean logs, every feature. Zeros get value , result dense. See Pseudocount . 'rclr': Robust centered log ratio: \(\log(x)\) minus mean log sample's non-zero counts, non-zero counts ; zeros stay 0. 'log': Log relative abundance (log-TSS): \(\log\) sample's proportions adding pseudocount every value, \(\log((x + pseudocount) / \sum (x + pseudocount))\). clr shifted one constant per sample. Zeros get value , result dense. See Pseudocount . 'none': transformation. margin margin containing samples. 1 samples rows, 2 samples columns. Ignored counts special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1 pseudocount Value added counts handle zeros norm = 'clr' 'log'. Ignored normalization methods. title: Symmetric Proportionality — phi_s
text: \(z\) log-ratio-transformed abundances (clr alr), $$\phi_{s,ij} = \frac{\mathrm{var}(z_i - z_j)}{\mathrm{var}(z_i + z_j)} = \frac{1 - \rho_{p,ij}}{1 + \rho_{p,ij}}$$ \(\mathrm{var}(z_i - z_j)\) vlr() \(\rho_p\) rho_p(). lies \([0, \infty)\): 0 proportional features, 1 unrelated ones, infinite reciprocal ones (\(z_i = -z_j\)). computed \(\mathrm{vlr}_{ij} / (2\mathrm{var}(z_i) + 2\mathrm{var}(z_j) - \mathrm{vlr}_{ij})\), since \(\mathrm{var}(+ b) = 2\mathrm{var}() + 2\mathrm{var}(b) - \mathrm{var}(- b)\). Unlike vlr(), depends denominator. Near-reciprocal pairs (two features two-feature denominator, whose \(z\) exact opposites) \(\mathrm{var}(z_i + z_j)\) near 0, rounding dominates: value Inf merely large. Lovell et al.'s (2015) original \(\phi = \mathrm{vlr}_{ij} / \mathrm{var}(z_i)\) symmetric (\(\phi_{ij} \ne \phi_{ji}\)), dist; Quinn et al. (2017) replaced \(\phi_s\). measure propr computes propr(counts, metric = "phs") (see Zeros zero handling).

code: # Colour by a column of metadata, with a legend.     ord <- pcoa(bray(iris[, 1:4]))     plot(ord, 'Species', iris)       # The third axis instead of the second.     plot(ord, 'Species', iris, axes = c(1, 3))       # A PCA biplot: the loadings as arrows.     plot(pca(iris[, 1:4], scale = TRUE), iris$Species)       # A compositional (covariance) biplot, with links whose lengths     # approximate the standard deviations of log ratios.     ord <- pca(ex_counts, norm = 'clr', pseudocount = 1)     plot(ord, scaling = 'covariance',          links = c('Streptococcus', 'Bacteroides', 'Corynebacterium'))       # The features that contribute most to the plane.     plot(ord, scaling = 'contribution')       # vegan's scaling 1 of an RDA.     plot(rda(iris[, 1:4]), iris$Species, scaling = 1)       # A constrained ordination: centroids of each species, and an arrow     # for the numeric constraint.     ord <- rda(iris[, 1:4], data = iris, formula = ~ Species + Sepal.Width)     plot(ord, 'Species', iris)       # Supervised methods colour by their own groups.     plot(lda(iris[, 1:4], 'Species', iris))       # The features ranked by their loadings on the first axis.     plot(pca(iris[, 1:4], scale = TRUE), type = 'rank')       # Any argument of plot() still works.     plot(nmds(bray(iris[, 1:4]), seed = 1), col = 'grey40', main = 'NMDS')

Fitting stops early, warning, \(X_a^T Y_a\) falls \(\sqrt{\epsilon} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\) times value first component: left table covariance groups, beyond rounding error (instance, components span whole table). title: Robust Aitchison distance — robust_aitchison
text: Robust Aitchison distance defined : $$\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^{n} (X^*_i - Y^*_i)^2}$$ : \(X^*_i\), \(Y^*_i\) : rclr-transformed counts \(\)-th feature. given sample \(X\), \(X^*_i = \ln(X_i) - X_L\) \(X_i > 0\), \(0\) otherwise. \(X_L\), \(Y_L\) : Mean log strictly positive abundances. \(X_L = \frac{1}{|P_X|}\sum_{j \P_X} \ln{X_j}\), \(P_X\) set indices \(X > 0\). \(|P_X|\), \(|P_Y|\) : number strictly positive features respective samples. \(n\) : total number features. Base R Equivalent:   Sequencing depth. uses robust clr rpca(), caveat sequencing depth applies : inference, since Schloss (2026) benchmarked robust Aitchison PCA, distance alone. See "Sequencing depth" rpca() check, beta_div_rarefied() rarefied alternative.

code: # Two source environments, three samples of each, and three sinks:     # a mix of soil and water, mostly soil, and mostly something else.     soil  <- c(300, 200, 100, 50, 0, 0, 0, 0)     water <- c(0, 0, 50, 100, 200, 300, 0, 0)     other <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 300, 350)     counts <- rbind(       soil1  = soil + c(10, 0, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),       soil2  = soil + c(0, 20, 0, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0),       soil3  = soil,       water1 = water + c(0, 0, 0, 0, 10, 0, 0, 0),       water2 = water + c(0, 0, 0, 10, 0, 20, 0, 0),       water3 = water,       mix    = soil + water,       soily  = 3 * soil + water,       novel  = soil + 5 * other )     sources <- c(rep('soil', 3), rep('water', 3), NA, NA, NA)      st <- sourcetracker(counts, sources, depth = 500, n_burnin = 20)     st #> # A matrix: 3 sinks × 3 sources #> # Source contributions (SourceTracker) #> # Mean of 10 draws #>         soil  water Unknown #> mix   0.509  0.429    0.062 #> soily 0.675  0.262    0.063 #> novel 0.0184 0.0012   0.98 #> # Attributes: sd, n_draws, method      plot(st)       # Leave one out: how distinct are the environments?     sourcetracker(counts, sources, depth = 500, n_burnin = 20, loo = TRUE) #> # A matrix: 2 sinks × 3 sources #> # Source contributions (SourceTracker) #> # Mean of 10 draws #>         soil  water Unknown #> soil  0      0.0062   0.994 #> water 0.0054 0        0.995 #> # Attributes: sd, n_draws, method
